COLDWAR_SOV_the_peace_programme: At the Twenty-Fourth Party Congress in the spring of 1971, Leonid Brezhnev unveils a Peace Programme that recasts Soviet foreign policy around peaceful coexistence. Recognition of Europe's post-war borders, arms limitation and expanded trade with the capitalist world are to secure what decades of confrontation could not. The treaty signed with Bonn in August 1970 already points the way; now the whole Politburo must commit to detente.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_berlin_agreement: West Berlin remains the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe, an island of the West deep inside the German Democratic Republic. Ambassador Pyotr Abrasimov sits down with his American, British and French counterparts to settle access routes, transit rights and the city's ties to the Federal Republic. A Quadripartite Agreement would defuse a crisis that has flared repeatedly since 1948, but East Berlin fears that Moscow is trading away its interests for detente.
COLDWAR_SOV_salt_negotiations: Since November 1969 Soviet and American delegations have been meeting in Helsinki and Vienna to discuss limits on strategic weapons. Vladimir Semyonov's team must reconcile the hopes of the Foreign Ministry with the deep suspicions of the General Staff and the defence industry. Now that rough parity with the United States is within reach, Moscow must decide whether to freeze the race through negotiation or press on towards outright strategic superiority.
COLDWAR_SOV_salt_i_and_the_abm_treaty: In May 1972, beneath the chandeliers of the Kremlin, Leonid Brezhnev and Richard Nixon are ready to sign the first agreements limiting the nuclear arsenals of the superpowers. The Interim Agreement freezes the number of missile launchers, while the ABM Treaty restricts each side to minimal missile defences. For the marshals it is a constraint on Soviet power; for the Politburo it is formal recognition that the USSR stands as America's equal.
COLDWAR_SOV_superiority_not_parity: Marshal Andrei Grechko and the Central Committee's defence secretary Dmitry Ustinov argue that arms control merely freezes American advantages in technology. With a new generation of heavy missiles nearing deployment, they insist the Soviet Union can win the arms race outright if it keeps building. Abandoning the talks would delight the General Staff and the design bureaus, but it would also commit the economy to a ruinous competition with no end in sight.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_moscow_summit: No American president has ever made an official visit to Moscow. A summit with Richard Nixon would crown the policy of detente and could produce a joint declaration of Basic Principles governing relations between the two superpowers, pledging restraint and peaceful coexistence. Despite the American bombing of North Vietnam, Brezhnev is determined that the visit should go ahead, convinced that recognition as an equal is worth the indignation of Hanoi.
COLDWAR_SOV_trade_and_credits: The Volga automobile plant at Togliatti, built with the help of Fiat, has shown what Western machinery and loans can achieve. Alexei Kosygin and the Ministry of Foreign Trade now seek credits from Western banks, licences and entire factories to modernise Soviet industry, paying with oil, gas and timber. The ideologues warn of dependence on capitalist creditors, but the planners see no faster way to close the technological gap.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_paris_axis: Since de Gaulle's visit in 1966, France has been the Western power most willing to deal with Moscow on its own terms. President Georges Pompidou's visit in October 1970 offers the chance to deepen this special relationship through regular political consultations, joint research and industrial cooperation, from colour television to space science. A privileged partnership with Paris would show Washington that Western Europe need not follow American leadership in everything.
COLDWAR_SOV_vladivostok_accords: The first SALT agreements will expire in 1977, and a permanent treaty is needed to replace them. Meeting the new American president Gerald Ford near Vladivostok in November 1974, Brezhnev can agree on a framework of equal ceilings for strategic launchers and multiple warheads. The marshals grumble that American forward-based systems in Europe are left untouched, but a deal would keep detente alive after the fall of Nixon.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_helsinki_conference: For a quarter of a century Moscow has sought formal recognition of the borders drawn in 1945. The Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, gathering thirty-five states in Helsinki, can finally deliver it. The price is the so-called Third Basket on human contacts, information and human rights. Gromyko considers it a harmless concession on paper, yet dissidents across the Union are already preparing to hold the Soviet state to its signature.
COLDWAR_SOV_salt_ii: After years of haggling over warhead limits, cruise missiles and the Backfire bomber, a second strategic arms treaty is finally ready. In Vienna in June 1979, Brezhnev and Jimmy Carter can sign SALT II, setting equal limits on launchers and multiple warheads until 1985. The treaty would cap the arms race at a costly but stable level, provided the American Senate ever agrees to ratify it.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_end_of_detente: Detente is unravelling. Soviet involvement in Africa, the deployment of new SS-20 missiles in Europe and NATO's answer with Pershing and cruise missiles have poisoned relations with Washington. The Politburo must decide whether the policy of the Peace Programme can still be rescued through concessions, or whether the time has come to accept a renewed confrontation with the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_save_detente: Detente has brought recognition, trade and grain, and Moscow is not prepared to throw it away. Through new proposals on arms control, restraint in the Third World and personal letters to the American president, the Soviet leadership tries to rebuild trust before the hardliners in both capitals bury the policy for good. Such gestures cost prestige at home, and the generals will see them as weakness.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_second_cold_war: Washington has chosen confrontation, and Moscow will not be intimidated. The SS-20s stay in Europe, the military budget grows, and Soviet propaganda denounces the new American arms build-up as preparation for nuclear war. The years of summits and handshakes are over; the Soviet Union returns to the logic of the Cold War, convinced that only strength commands the respect of its adversaries.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_chinese_question: Less than a year ago Soviet and Chinese soldiers fought pitched battles on Damansky Island in the Ussuri and at Tielieketi on the Xinjiang border. Beijing now calls the Soviet Union social-imperialist and its main enemy, while Moscow fears a nuclear-armed China of eight hundred million people along a frontier thousands of kilometres long. How to deal with Mao's China has become the most pressing security question facing the Politburo.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_beijing_border_talks: After Alexei Kosygin's hurried meeting with Zhou Enlai at Beijing airport in September 1969, both sides have agreed to talk. Since October, First Deputy Foreign Minister Vasily Kuznetsov has led a delegation in Beijing to negotiate the disputed border and avoid new clashes. Progress is slow and the rhetoric remains hostile, but every month of talks is a month without fighting on the Ussuri.
COLDWAR_SOV_three_roads_to_beijing: The General Staff, the Foreign Ministry and the International Department each offer a different answer to the Chinese challenge. Moscow can contain China with a wall of divisions and alliances, strike its nuclear programme before it matures, or seek a reconciliation that would reunite the two great communist powers. Each road carries its own risks, and the choice will shape Soviet policy in Asia for decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_contain_china: The Soviet Union will neither attack China nor bow to its demands. Instead, the frontier from the Pamirs to the Pacific is to become a defensive barrier, backed by a network of friendly states around China's periphery. Containment is expensive and slow, but it promises security without the risk of a nuclear war in Asia, and it leaves the door open for talks once Beijing becomes more reasonable.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_trans_baikal_buildup: Between 1969 and 1972 the Soviet forces facing China are to grow from a modest screen into a powerful front. New garrisons, airfields and depots are rising across the Trans-Baikal and Far Eastern Military Districts, while tank and motor-rifle divisions move east along the Trans-Siberian Railway. The buildup consumes enormous resources, but it ensures that the People's Liberation Army will never repeat Damansky on a larger scale.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_amur_fortified_districts: Along the Amur and the Ussuri, where the border runs within sight of Chinese villages, the army is constructing fortified districts of bunkers, gun emplacements and dug-in tank turrets. Manned by machine-gun and artillery units, these defences are meant to blunt any Chinese offensive long enough for reserves to arrive from the west. Khabarovsk and Blagoveshchensk, both within artillery range of China, depend on them.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_mongolian_shield: Mongolia guards the shortest route from northern China to Lake Baikal and the Trans-Siberian Railway. Under the treaty of 1966, Moscow can station the 39th Army in the country and turn the Mongolian People's Republic into a forward bastion against China. Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal's government is willing, but Ulaanbaatar expects economic aid in return for hosting Soviet tanks and airfields.
COLDWAR_SOV_asian_collective_security: In June 1969 Leonid Brezhnev proposed a system of collective security in Asia, a vague idea that everyone in the region understood to be aimed at China. Reviving the proposal would bind India, Vietnam, Mongolia and Afghanistan more closely to Moscow and present the Soviet Union as the guarantor of peace in Asia. Beijing will denounce it as encirclement, but China's wary neighbours may find the offer attractive.
COLDWAR_SOV_treaty_with_india: As the crisis in East Pakistan escalates and Washington moves closer to Beijing and Islamabad, Indira Gandhi's government seeks a reliable partner. A Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation, prepared by Andrei Gromyko and Swaran Singh, would make India the cornerstone of Soviet policy in South Asia and a counterweight to China. In return, Moscow must be ready to supply weapons and diplomatic cover should war break out.
COLDWAR_SOV_vietnam_against_china: Vietnam, increasingly at odds with Beijing, has become China's southern rival. A Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with Hanoi would grant the Soviet Navy access to the great American-built base at Cam Ranh Bay and open a second front against China in the south. Yet the alliance could drag Moscow into a war over Cambodia, where Vietnam and China's protege Pol Pot are already clashing.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_surgical_strike_option: In 1969 Soviet diplomats quietly asked their American contacts how Washington would react to a strike on China's nuclear facilities. Some in the General Staff still believe that a single blow could destroy Mao's atomic programme before it can threaten Soviet cities. What if the option, never formally adopted, were taken seriously? The Politburo must decide whether to keep it on the table.
COLDWAR_SOV_plan_lop_nur: The planners of the General Staff draw up detailed options for a strike on the Chinese nuclear test site at Lop Nur and the weapons facilities around it. Missile brigades and long-range aviation are assigned targets, while ground forces prepare to exploit the chaos that would follow. The plan gives Moscow the means to topple the Maoist regime, but the decision to use it would be the gravest in Soviet history.
COLDWAR_SOV_strike_at_dawn: Orders are drafted for a strike at dawn: missiles and bombers against Lop Nur and China's nuclear infrastructure, tank armies in Mongolia and the Trans-Baikal ready to roll into Manchuria and Xinjiang. Moscow prepares to present the operation as a preventive measure against Maoist adventurism, but news of the preparations is already causing alarm in Washington, Delhi and Tokyo. Once the order is given, there is no way back.
COLDWAR_SOV_reconcile_with_beijing: What if the meeting between Kosygin and Zhou Enlai at Beijing airport in September 1969 had been a turning point rather than a mere ceasefire? An ideological truce, an end to the polemics between the two parties and a pullback of forces from the border could restore the alliance broken in the early 1960s. The hardliners in both capitals will resist, but a united communist world would transform the balance of the Cold War.
COLDWAR_SOV_settle_damansky: The bloody island of Damansky, which the Chinese call Zhenbao, lies on the Chinese side of the main channel of the Ussuri. Accepting the river's navigable channel as the border, as international practice suggests, would hand the island to China and remove the most visible symbol of the conflict. Historically the question was settled only in 1991; doing it now would show Beijing that Moscow is serious about peace.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_eastern_front_secured: Whether through strength or through compromise, the danger of a great war with China has receded. The divisions in the Far East can be held at a sustainable level, the frontier regions can turn to development, and the Baikal-Amur Mainline will one day connect Siberia's riches with the Pacific. For the first time since 1969, the Soviet Union can look east without fear.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_socialist_commonwealth: Moscow speaks of a socialist commonwealth, a family of fraternal states bound together by Marxism-Leninism, the Warsaw Pact and Comecon. Behind the rhetoric lies a reality of Soviet garrisons in Central Europe, cheap raw materials flowing west and growing frustration in Warsaw, Budapest and Bucharest. Keeping the commonwealth united requires constant attention, generosity and, when necessary, pressure.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_doctrine_question: The tanks that rolled into Prague in August 1968 raised a question that still hangs over the Eastern bloc: how sovereign are the socialist states? Moscow can enshrine the right to intervene whenever socialism is threatened, or it can accept that each fraternal party must find its own way, with all the risks that entails. The answer will define relations with Eastern Europe for a generation.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_brezhnev_doctrine: In September 1968 Pravda declared that the sovereignty of each socialist country is limited by the interests of the socialist community as a whole. Making this principle the formal basis of bloc policy tells every party leader from East Berlin to Sofia that no one may leave the camp. Western governments will see it as proof that detente stops at the Elbe, but for Moscow the unity of the bloc comes first.
COLDWAR_SOV_let_them_go_their_way: What if Moscow announced, twenty years early, that each socialist country may choose its own path? The Politburo could renounce the use of force against its allies and allow reformers like those of the Prague Spring to experiment freely. Eastern Europe would gain new legitimacy and the West would applaud, but the hardliners warn that once the doors are open, the whole bloc may walk through them.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_comprehensive_programme: At the Comecon session in Bucharest in July 1971, the member states are to adopt a Comprehensive Programme for socialist economic integration. Joint investment projects, coordinated five-year plans, specialisation of production and cooperation in science are meant to turn a loose trading club into an integrated economic bloc. Romania insists on its sovereignty, but most partners welcome Soviet resources and markets.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_oil_price_question: Soviet oil flows to Eastern Europe through the Druzhba pipeline at prices far below the world market. This subsidy keeps the economies of the fraternal states running and buys their loyalty, but every barrel sold cheaply in Leipzig or Bratislava is a barrel that could earn hard currency in Rotterdam. As world prices climb, the question of what fraternal oil should cost can no longer be avoided.
COLDWAR_SOV_subsidised_oil: Moscow decides that the stability of its allies is worth more than hard currency. Oil and gas will continue to flow to Comecon partners at friendly prices, cushioning Poland and the German Democratic Republic from the shocks of the world economy. The Ministry of Finance counts the lost revenue, but the Politburo knows that a hungry, cold Eastern Europe would cost far more.
COLDWAR_SOV_world_market_prices: The Bucharest formula of 1975 tied Comecon oil prices to a moving average of world prices; what if Moscow went all the way? Charging the fraternal states the full market rate would bring substantial additional revenue and end the hidden subsidy to Eastern Europe. Warsaw, East Berlin and Prague will protest loudly, and their already strained economies may not survive the shock.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soyuz_pipeline: The gas fields of Orenburg could supply Eastern Europe for decades, if only a pipeline to the western border can be built. Moscow proposes that each Comecon partner construct its own section of the Soyuz line in exchange for guaranteed gas deliveries. The project would weld the bloc together with steel and gas, a monument to socialist economic integration stretching across the steppe and the Ukrainian plains.
COLDWAR_SOV_shield_and_brotherhood: Large joint manoeuvres demonstrate the unity and readiness of the Warsaw Pact. Exercises such as Brotherhood in Arms, held in the German Democratic Republic in 1970, and the Shield series bring together armies from the Baltic to the Black Sea under Soviet direction. Each exercise must be agreed with the allied governments, but the shared experience strengthens both the coalition and the Soviet Army itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_kulikovs_unified_command: The Unified Armed Forces of the Warsaw Pact are still more a coalition on paper than an integrated force. Under a forceful commander-in-chief such as Marshal Viktor Kulikov, a permanent staff, common doctrine and shared research could transform them into a single military machine. The allies will gain access to Soviet expertise, but they will also find their armies ever more closely bound to Moscow's plans.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_polish_question: In December 1970 sudden price increases just before Christmas drive the shipyard workers of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin into the streets. The militia opens fire, dozens are killed, and Władysław Gomułka falls, replaced by the Silesian party boss Edward Gierek. Moscow must decide how to handle Poland: rescue the new leadership with money and grain, or remind Warsaw firmly where its obligations lie.
COLDWAR_SOV_credits_for_gierek: Edward Gierek promises the Polish workers a better life, but he needs money and grain to deliver it. Moscow can extend credits, raw materials and food to stabilise his government and calm the shipyards. The help is expensive, and Gierek will soon be borrowing from Western banks as well, yet a stable Poland is the keystone of the Warsaw Pact and the corridor to the Soviet forces in Germany.
COLDWAR_SOV_discipline_warsaw: The Polish comrades have let the situation slip out of control, and Moscow will not reward failure. The Polish leadership is summoned to the Kremlin to hear unambiguous demands for ideological firmness, order in the shipyards and loyalty to the alliance. How Warsaw answers is up to the Poles, but every party leader in the bloc will understand the message.
COLDWAR_SOV_romanias_maverick_course: Nicolae Ceaușescu refused to join the invasion of Czechoslovakia, recognised West Germany, kept relations with Israel and welcomed Richard Nixon to Bucharest in 1969. Romania remains a member of the Warsaw Pact and Comecon, yet it behaves more and more like a non-aligned state. Moscow must decide whether to tolerate this independent streak or to make an example of Bucharest.
COLDWAR_SOV_tolerate_bucharest: Ceaușescu's independence is irritating, but Romania remains a one-party communist state with no intention of leaving the bloc. Moscow chooses to swallow its pride, keep the dialogue open and let Bucharest enjoy its moments on the world stage. Tolerance spares the alliance a damaging quarrel and frees the leadership to concentrate on more pressing matters.
COLDWAR_SOV_isolate_bucharest: Romania's flirtation with Washington and Beijing can no longer be tolerated. Moscow will freeze joint projects, cool party contacts and make clear to the other allies that independence has its price. The pressure may push Ceaușescu even closer to the West and China, but it will show the rest of the bloc exactly where the limits lie.
COLDWAR_SOV_interkosmos: Since 1967 the Interkosmos programme has allowed Soviet allies to share in the conquest of space through joint satellites and scientific experiments. The next step is to fly guest cosmonauts from fraternal countries aboard Soyuz spacecraft to the Salyut stations. A Czechoslovak, Polish, East German, Cuban or Vietnamese cosmonaut in orbit would be a powerful symbol of socialist solidarity and of Soviet leadership in space.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_commonwealth_of_socialis: What if the loose web of treaties binding the Eastern bloc were replaced by a formal Commonwealth of Socialist Nations? Permanent common institutions, coordinated planning and joint aid programmes could give the alliance a structure as solid as the European Community in the West. Smaller allies fear absorption into a Soviet superstate, but the advocates argue that only true integration can match the economic power of the capitalist world.
COLDWAR_SOV_proletarian_internationalism: Lenin taught that the cause of socialism knows no borders, and the Soviet Union regards itself as the bulwark of national liberation movements around the world. Through the International Department of the Central Committee under Boris Ponomarev, Moscow supports communist parties, liberation fronts and progressive regimes in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Solidarity is a duty, but it is also a powerful instrument of Soviet influence.
COLDWAR_SOV_operation_kavkaz: Israeli deep-penetration raids are striking at the heart of Egypt, and Gamal Abdel Nasser flies secretly to Moscow to plead for help. Under Operation Kavkaz, an entire air defence division with modern surface-to-air missiles and squadrons of MiG-21s flown by Soviet pilots can be deployed along the Suez Canal. It would be one of the largest Soviet combat deployments outside the bloc, and a direct challenge to Israel and its American patrons.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_treaty_with_egypt: After the death of Nasser in September 1970, Moscow is anxious to bind his successor Anwar Sadat to the Soviet camp. A Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation, signed in Cairo in May 1971, would formalise the presence of thousands of Soviet advisers and the flow of arms to the most important state in the Arab world. Sadat's loyalty is uncertain, but Egypt remains the key to Soviet influence in the Middle East.
COLDWAR_SOV_lifeline_to_hanoi: North Vietnam's war against the United States and Saigon depends on Soviet surface-to-air missiles, MiG fighters, fuel and rice delivered through Haiphong and across China. Expanding this lifeline would strengthen Hanoi's defences against American bombing and secure Soviet influence over the Vietnamese communists, who are courted by Beijing as well. The supplies will anger Washington, but abandoning a fraternal party at war is unthinkable.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_island_of_freedom: Cuba is the Soviet outpost in the Western Hemisphere, but its economy is reeling after the failed ten-million-ton sugar harvest of 1970. By buying Cuban sugar at preferential prices and supplying oil in return, Moscow can keep Fidel Castro's revolution afloat and bind the island to Comecon. The subsidy is expensive, but a socialist Cuba ninety miles from Florida is worth every rouble.
COLDWAR_SOV_syria_and_iraq: The Baathist regimes in Damascus and Baghdad are bitter rivals of each other, yet both are natural partners for Moscow. Iraq is ready to sign a Treaty of Friendship and needs Soviet help to nationalise its oil industry, while Hafez al-Assad's Syria seeks weapons and advisers to rebuild its army. Together they would give the Soviet Union a firm foothold in the Middle East, whatever happens in Cairo.
COLDWAR_SOV_patrice_lumumba_university: Founded in Moscow in 1960, the Peoples' Friendship University named after Patrice Lumumba educates thousands of students from Asia, Africa and Latin America. Expanding it would train a new generation of engineers, doctors and party cadres who return home with Soviet diplomas and, it is hoped, Soviet sympathies. Not every graduate becomes a friend of Moscow, but the investment in future elites pays off over decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_military_advisers: From Egypt to Vietnam, Soviet officers train armies, operate radar stations and teach the use of modern weapons. A permanent corps of military advisers, organised through the Tenth Main Directorate of the General Staff, would make Soviet assistance more efficient and more influential. Advisers on the ground often achieve more than arms shipments alone, and they let Moscow know exactly what its partners are doing.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_question_of_aid: Every partner in the Third World asks for help, but Soviet resources are not unlimited. Moscow can build dams, steel mills and power stations as it did at Aswan and Bhilai, winning goodwill through visible development, or it can concentrate on weapons, which are cheaper to provide and buy influence with the generals who often hold real power. The choice will define the character of Soviet engagement in the developing world.
COLDWAR_SOV_economic_aid_programmes: The Aswan High Dam remains the proudest symbol of Soviet friendship in the Third World. By expanding economic aid programmes, from the Euphrates dam in Syria to steelworks in India, Moscow can show that socialism brings not only weapons but development. Such projects take years and consume scarce resources, yet they leave lasting monuments and tie entire economies to Soviet technology and expertise.
COLDWAR_SOV_arms_on_credit: Tanks, fighters and missiles are the Soviet Union's most sought-after exports. Selling them on generous credit terms, often never fully repaid, wins the gratitude of governments and armies across the Middle East, Africa and Asia. The defence industry welcomes the orders, and every customer becomes dependent on Soviet spare parts, ammunition and instructors for years to come.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_cuban_bridge: As Portugal's empire collapses, the Marxist MPLA of Agostinho Neto fights rival movements backed by Zaire, South Africa and the United States for control of Angola. Fidel Castro is ready to send Cuban troops, but only Soviet aircraft and weapons can carry and equip them across the Atlantic. Supporting this bridge would establish a new socialist state in southern Africa, at the cost of further damage to detente.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_horn_of_africa: In the Horn of Africa, Moscow has two clients who are about to go to war with each other. Siad Barre's Somalia hosts a Soviet naval facility at Berbera, while the revolutionary Derg in Ethiopia under Mengistu Haile Mariam proclaims Marxism-Leninism. When Somalia moves to seize the Ogaden, the Soviet Union will have to choose one side and lose the other.
COLDWAR_SOV_back_ethiopia: Ethiopia, with its large population and revolutionary government, is the greater prize. Moscow can organise a massive airlift of weapons and send General Vasily Petrov to direct the defence of the Ogaden alongside Cuban brigades. The decision will cost the base at Berbera and the friendship of Somalia, but it could secure a loyal Marxist-Leninist ally on the Red Sea.
COLDWAR_SOV_back_somalia: Somalia has been a faithful partner for years and hosts the valuable naval facility at Berbera. Continuing to arm Siad Barre's army would keep this foothold on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, even as Somali forces advance into the Ogaden. Abandoning the revolutionaries in Addis Ababa would hurt Soviet prestige among African progressives, but a loyal ally in hand may be worth more than a promise.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_afghan_question: In April 1978 the Saur Revolution brought the communist People's Democratic Party to power in Kabul, but its radical reforms have provoked rebellion across the country. In March 1979 an uprising in Herat killed Soviet advisers, and Nur Muhammad Taraki is begging for troops. The Politburo must decide whether to intervene directly or leave the Afghan comrades to fight their own war.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_limited_contingent: If the Afghan government formally asks for help, the Soviet Union can send a Limited Contingent of troops to secure the cities, roads and airfields while the Afghan army fights the rebels. Andropov, Ustinov and Gromyko believe a short intervention will stabilise the regime and keep Afghanistan out of American hands. The world will condemn the move, and no one can say how long the soldiers will have to stay.
COLDWAR_SOV_no_soviet_soldier: In March 1979 Alexei Kosygin told Taraki on the telephone that Soviet troops could not replace the Afghan people in their own struggle. What if the leadership had held to his advice? Kabul would receive weapons, advisers and money, but not a single Soviet soldier. The Afghan communists will feel betrayed, yet the Soviet Union spares itself a war in the mountains that could last for years.
COLDWAR_SOV_vanguard_of_world_revolution: What if Moscow abandoned caution and openly embraced the role of vanguard of world revolution? Liberation movements from southern Africa to Central America would receive weapons, money and training without the restraint imposed by detente. The cost to the Soviet budget and to relations with the West would be immense, but the ideologues dream of a world where the correlation of forces has shifted decisively towards socialism.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_the_party_of_a_new_type: Lenin conceived the Bolsheviks as a party of a new type: disciplined, centralised and guided by revolutionary theory. Restoring this spirit means weeding out careerists, raising ideological standards and demanding exemplary conduct from every member. The Communist Party of the Soviet Union would once again lead by example rather than by inertia, and its authority among the people would grow accordingly.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_komsomol_mobilisation: The Komsomol counts tens of millions of young members, many of whom have never felt the enthusiasm of the founding years. Shock construction projects in Siberia, student work brigades and military-patriotic education can mobilise this energy for the building of communism. A generation that lays track across the taiga will also stand ready to defend the motherland.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_the_workers_state: The Soviet Union calls itself the state of workers and peasants, yet the people on the factory floor often feel far removed from the decisions made in their name. Giving the trade unions a stronger voice, improving working conditions and honouring labour in culture and propaganda can renew the bond between the party and the working class. The ideals of October must be visible in every workshop.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_the_cpsu: Whatever factions may have risen in recent years, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union claims to be the only true heir of Lenin. Placing power firmly back in the hands of the CPSU under Leonid Brezhnev would restore the familiar order of the Politburo, the Central Committee and the regional committees. The transition will unsettle the ministries for a time, but it promises continuity and a return to the Leninist norms of party life.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_councils: What if the old slogan of 1917 were taken literally? The Free Councils of Labour, led by Pyotr Siuda, a veteran of the Novocherkassk strike of 1962, demand that power pass from the party apparatus to elected councils of workers in every factory and town. The experiment would dismantle the nomenklatura and could unleash enormous energy, or plunge the economy into chaos.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_iron_line: For the Neo-Stalinist Platform, the troubles of the Soviet Union stem from the abandonment of Stalin's firm hand. Led by Sergei Trapeznikov, the Central Committee's conservative chief of science and education, the Iron Line promises discipline, ideological vigilance and an end to the half-hearted experiments of recent years. Handing them power would reassure the hardliners in the army and the security organs, but it would chill the intelligentsia and alarm the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_komsomol: Alexander Shelepin, former head of the Komsomol and the KGB, has never abandoned his ambition to lead the Soviet Union. His Komsomol Vanguard gathers a younger generation of officials who promise energy, order and a decisive break with the ageing men of the Politburo. Handing them power would be a generational revolution from above, carried out by men known for their authoritarian instincts.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_the_leading_role_of_the_p: Whatever the course of recent events, the Communist Party remains the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, the nucleus of its political system and of all state and public organisations. Reaffirming this principle, which a new constitution will enshrine in its sixth article, gives the party apparatus a clear mandate to direct the state. It is the foundation on which every further reform or consolidation must rest.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_socialist_emulation: Socialist emulation pits brigades, workshops and factories against one another in comradely competition to exceed the plan. Red banners, honour boards and the title of Hero of Socialist Labour reward the best, while laggards are criticised in the factory newspaper. Freeing the movement from formalism and empty pledges can raise efficiency and morale without abandoning the principles of planning.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_peoples_control: The Committee of People's Control, with millions of volunteer inspectors in every factory, office and collective farm, is meant to be the eyes of the working people over the bureaucracy. Giving it real powers to investigate embezzlement, waste and abuse of office would strike at the corruption spreading through the apparatus. The nomenklatura will resent the scrutiny, but honest citizens will welcome it.
COLDWAR_SOV_em_peace_and_socialism: From its editorial offices in Prague, the journal Problems of Peace and Socialism brings together communist and workers' parties from around the world. Turning it into a genuine platform for the international movement would carry the Soviet vision of socialism far beyond the bloc and strengthen ties with fraternal parties in the West and the Third World. A shared voice is the first step towards a shared strategy.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_the_samizdat_presses: Typed on carbon paper and passed from hand to hand, samizdat carries forbidden novels, poetry and the Chronicle of Current Events across the Soviet Union. Instead of hunting down every typewriter, the authorities could simply look the other way. Tolerating the underground presses would win the trust of the intelligentsia and open a channel for honest criticism, though the ideological guardians warn that it is the first crack in the dam.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_stop_the_jamming: Every night a vast network of transmitters jams the Russian-language broadcasts of the Voice of America, the BBC and other Western stations. In September 1973, as a gesture of detente, the jamming of several of them was suspended. Ending it for good would save enormous sums, please Western governments and let Soviet citizens hear the world, but it would also break the party's monopoly on information.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_recognise_the_human_right: In November 1970 Andrei Sakharov, Valery Chalidze and Andrei Tverdokhlebov founded the Human Rights Committee to study how Soviet law could protect the rights of citizens. The KGB regards them as enemies, but recognising the committee as a legitimate voice would demonstrate that Soviet socialism respects its own constitution. Such a step would earn praise abroad and enrage the security organs at home.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_systems_men: Dzhermen Gvishiani, deputy chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology and son-in-law of Alexei Kosygin, champions management science, systems analysis and computerised planning. His Systems Directorate envisions a Soviet Union governed by experts and data rather than by party dogma. Handing them power would mean leaving the party state behind entirely, a revolution of technocrats that could modernise the country or tear it apart.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_solidarists: For decades the People's Labour Union, known as the NTS, has waged a propaganda war against the Soviet regime from exile, smuggling its journals Posev and Grani into the country. Under Vladimir Poremsky it offers a vision of a national, Christian and solidarist Russia freed from communism. Bringing the émigrés home to power would be an unprecedented break with more than half a century of Soviet history.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_human_rights: The physicist Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb and now the country's most famous dissident, would lead a government founded on law, human rights and convergence with the West. The Committee for Human Rights promises to free political prisoners, end censorship and guarantee the freedom to emigrate. Such a transfer of power would astonish the world, though the security organs and much of the apparatus would never accept it willingly.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_democratic_socialists: The historian Roy Medvedev, author of a damning study of Stalinism, argues that the Soviet Union can be democratised without abandoning socialism. His Union of Democratic Socialists calls for free debate, competing candidates and an independent judiciary while preserving public ownership. Handing them power would turn the country into a socialist democracy, an experiment that Prague was never allowed to complete.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_a_democratic_union: With the monopoly of the party broken, the Soviet Union must rebuild itself as a democratic state. Freedom of speech and assembly, independent courts and genuine parliamentary institutions are to replace the old structures of control. The transition promises a flowering of science and public life, but it also releases grievances that decades of repression had kept hidden.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_free_elections: For the first time since the Constituent Assembly was dispersed in January 1918, the peoples of the Soviet Union are to choose their representatives freely among competing parties. Regular elections will give the new government genuine legitimacy and open the way for the human rights movement to win popular support. They will also give a voice to nationalists in the republics, who may use it to demand independence.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_the_market_returns: Central planning has failed to deliver the goods that Soviet citizens want. Private enterprise, free prices and foreign investment are to return after more than half a century of state monopoly, creating a mixed economy in which the state retains only the commanding heights. The reform promises growth and abundance, but in the short term it means rising prices, unemployment and widening inequality.
COLDWAR_SOV_we_join_the_free_world: The Soviet Union, once the leader of the socialist camp, is ready to change sides. Aligning with the United States and Western Europe would end the Cold War on terms no one in 1970 could have imagined, opening access to Western markets, credits and technology. For millions of veterans and party members it would be a bitter betrayal; for the new democrats it is the only path to a normal future.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_the_yugoslav_model: Josip Broz Tito's Yugoslavia has shown that socialism need not mean Soviet-style central planning. Workers' self-management, decentralised enterprises and a foreign policy independent of both blocs have brought Belgrade prosperity and international prestige. Studying the Yugoslav model, long condemned in Moscow as revisionism, would offer Soviet reformers an alternative that remains socialist without being Stalinist.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_the_technocrats: Economists, engineers and planners in the research institutes of Moscow and Novosibirsk believe that the Soviet economy can be fixed by expertise rather than ideology. They call for mathematical planning methods, profit incentives and the enterprise autonomy promised by the Kosygin reform of 1965. Giving them a voice would move the country towards a pragmatic course between the dogmas of the party and the models of the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_the_village_prose: Writers such as Valentin Rasputin, Vasily Belov and Vasily Shukshin mourn the dying Russian village, its traditions, its churches and its moral world, destroyed by collectivisation and industrial progress. Their village prose has become a quiet conservative counterculture, tolerated by the censors yet deeply critical of Soviet modernity. Encouraging this current would strengthen a rooted, national alternative to both communist and Western ideologies.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_the_third_force: Between the party loyalists and the Western-minded dissidents stands a third force: technocrats, conservatives and environmentalists who want reform without capitulation. Allowing them to organise and to influence policy would broaden the political spectrum and create allies for change within the system. The Politburo's conservatives see a dangerous dilution of the party line, but the reformers see a way out of stagnation.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_planners: Nikolai Baibakov has chaired the State Planning Committee since 1965 and knows the Soviet economy better than anyone. His Gosplan Technocracy would govern not through ideology or party congresses but through balances, targets and indicators. Handing power to the planners would put the economy before politics, creating an administrative state run by the men who actually manage the country's resources.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_solzhenitsyn: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Nobel laureate and chronicler of the Gulag, calls on his countrymen to live not by lies. His followers envision a Russia freed from communist ideology and rooted in Orthodox faith, rural values and the traditions of local self-government. Handing them power would be a moral revolution, but Solzhenitsyn's authoritarian streak and Russian nationalism trouble the non-Russian republics and the Westernisers alike.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_directors: The directors of the great factories, combines and ministries are the true masters of the Soviet economy, and they are tired of taking orders from party secretaries. With the backing of Interior Minister Nikolai Shchelokov, the Red Directors propose a government of managers in which the heads of industry hold power directly. Their rule might be efficient, and profitable for many of them, but it risks turning public property into private fiefdoms.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_free_enterprise: The economist Nikolai Shmelyov argues that the Soviet economy can be saved only by markets, private initiative and honest prices. His Free Enterprise League proposes dismantling the planning apparatus, legalising private business and opening the country to foreign investment. Handing them power would be a leap into the unknown, offering prosperity to the enterprising and hardship to those who have known nothing but the security of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_greens: Since the 1960s scientists and writers have fought to save Lake Baikal from the effluent of a giant pulp mill on its shore. Grigory Galazy, director of the Limnological Institute in Irkutsk, now leads the Friends of Baikal, grown into a broader movement against the environmental devastation caused by Soviet industry. A green government would put nature before production targets, a radical departure for a country built on heavy industry.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_market_socialists: Alexander Yakovlev, a party ideologist who studied in the United States and warned against Russian chauvinism, has come to believe that socialism needs markets to survive. His Socialist Market Commonwealth proposes combining public ownership with competition, enterprise autonomy and openness to the world. Handing them power would launch a far-reaching reform from within, one that could renew Soviet socialism or unravel it entirely.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_sovereign_republics: Pyotr Shelest, the former first secretary of the Ukrainian party, has long defended the economic and cultural rights of the republics against Moscow's centralism. His Union of Sovereign Republics proposes to turn the Soviet Union into a genuine federation in which each republic controls its own affairs. Handing them power would satisfy national aspirations from Kiev to Tashkent, but it could also loosen the bonds that hold the Union together.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_neither_moscow_nor_washin: The new Soviet leadership declares that the country will no longer head one bloc in a global confrontation. Neither the old Moscow of the Politburo nor Washington shall dictate the course of the world; instead the Soviet Union will pursue its own interests and keep an equal distance from all camps. It is a dramatic turn that leaves allies bewildered and opens entirely new possibilities for the country.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_the_third_way_economy: Between Soviet central planning and Western capitalism lies a third way. Inspired by the Kosygin reform, Yugoslav self-management and the ideas of the Czechoslovak economist Ota Šik, the new economic policy combines planning for key sectors with enterprise autonomy, market prices and trade with the whole world. It is an untested experiment on a continental scale, but its advocates believe it can unleash the potential stifled by decades of rigid planning.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_dissolve_the_pact: If the Soviet Union no longer leads a bloc, what is the purpose of the Warsaw Pact? Dissolving the alliance would free Eastern Europe to choose its own partners and remove the main justification for NATO's presence on the continent. Each former member will decide its own future, and some will certainly turn west, but the step would mark the true end of the post-war order in Europe.
COLDWAR_SOV_na_join_the_movement: Founded in Belgrade in 1961 by Tito, Nehru, Nasser and Sukarno, the Non-Aligned Movement brings together states that refuse to join either bloc. Seeking membership would be an astonishing step for a superpower, but it would align the Soviet Union with India and the developing world as an equal rather than a patron. The members will be wary of Moscow's motives, yet its accession would transform the movement overnight.
